title: Constructive IVT via Bisection Algorithm
description: Formalizes the constructive content of the Intermediate Value Theorem via the bisection algorithm. Proves the bisection interval halves in width each step ((b-a)/2^n), maintains the sign invariant f(left) ≤ 0 ≤ f(right), stays within [a,b], and — the main theorem — produces points x ∈ [a,b] with |f(x)| < ε for any ε > 0. Also proves uniqueness of the zero for strictly monotone f. 13 theorems, 3 definitions, 0 axioms.

meta.author: Lean Genius
meta.assumptions: None. Fully machine-verified using Mathlib's intermediate_value_Icc, uniformContinuousOn.
originalContributions: approx_ivt: for any ε > 0, bisection finds x ∈ [a,b] with |f(x)| < ε
bisect_width: after n steps, interval width = (b-a)/2^n (exact formula)
constructive_ivt_summary: packages approximate roots + midpoint containment + width → 0
monotone_ivt_unique: strict monotonicity implies unique zero

overview.historicalContext: The Intermediate Value Theorem was known informally to mathematicians since antiquity, but its precise statement and proof had to await the rigorous foundations of real analysis in the 19th century. Bolzano gave the first rigorous proof in 1817, and Cauchy refined it in his 1821 Cours d'analyse. The classical IVT is non-constructive: it asserts existence of a zero without providing a procedure to find it. The bisection algorithm, by contrast, has been known since at least the time of Archimedes (method of exhaustion) and provides an explicit approximation scheme. The key insight — that bisection on a compact interval converges because widths halve and uniform continuity gives f-value control — was made rigorous in the 20th century. In constructive mathematics (Bishop's program, 1967), the IVT is not provable in its classical form but the approximate version proven here holds constructively. This file gives a fully classical Lean proof of the constructive content.
overview.problemStatement: Given a continuous function $f: [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ with $f(a) \leq 0 \leq f(b)$, formalize the bisection algorithm and prove: (1) after $n$ steps the interval width is exactly $(b-a)/2^n$; (2) the sign invariant $f(l_n) \leq 0 \leq f(r_n)$ is maintained; (3) for any $\varepsilon > 0$ the algorithm finds $x \in [a,b]$ with $|f(x)| < \varepsilon$.
overview.text: The bisection step tests the midpoint: if $f(\text{mid}) \leq 0$, keep $[\text{mid}, \text{right}]$; otherwise keep $[\text{left}, \text{mid}]$. After $n$ steps the width is exactly $(b-a)/2^n$. The sign invariant $f(l_n) \leq 0 \leq f(r_n)$ is maintained throughout. For the approximate IVT: use uniform continuity on $[a,b]$ (compact, via `isCompact_Icc`) to find $\delta$ such that $|f(x)-f(y)| < \varepsilon$ when $|x-y| < \delta$; choose $n$ via `exists_pow_lt_of_lt_one` so $(b-a)/2^n < \delta$; the midpoint $x$ satisfies $\text{dist}(x, l_n) < \delta$ and $\text{dist}(x, r_n) < \delta$, so uniform continuity gives $|f(x) - f(l_n)| < \varepsilon$ and $|f(x) - f(r_n)| < \varepsilon$; since $f(l_n) \leq 0 \leq f(r_n)$ this forces $|f(x)| < \varepsilon$.
overview.proofStrategy: `bisect_width` by induction: step `bisectStep_width` (pure ring arithmetic, no induction). `bisect_sign` by induction using `bisectStep_sign` (split_ifs + push_neg). `approx_ivt`: extract $\delta$ from uniform continuity (`Metric.uniformContinuousOn_iff`), choose $n$ via `exists_pow_lt_of_lt_one`, establish `hwidth` (width < $\delta$), compute midpoint distances, apply `huc'` for both endpoints, combine with sign invariant via `abs_lt`.
keyInsights: Width halving: `bisectStep_width` is proved by pure ring arithmetic in one line — no induction needed because the formula $(p_2 - p_1)/2$ is immediate from the definition.
Sign preservation is the key loop invariant: at every stage $f(l_n) \leq 0 \leq f(r_n)$, guaranteeing by the classical IVT that a zero exists in $[l_n, r_n]$.

The critical bridge: uniform continuity of $f$ on the compact interval $[a,b]$ (by Heine-Cantor theorem) converts geometric closeness of points to closeness of function values, enabling the $\varepsilon$-bound.
The midpoint is within $(b-a)/2^{n+1}$ of both endpoints — both left AND right — which is the key to squeezing $|f(\text{mid})|$ between the two sign-opposite values.
The approximate IVT recovers the classical IVT: the bisection midpoints form a Cauchy sequence (widths $\to 0$) converging by completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ to an exact zero by continuity.
prerequisites: Uniform continuity on compact sets: Metric.uniformContinuousOn_iff

conclusion.summary: Machine-verifies the constructive content of the IVT: bisection on $[a,b]$ with width exactly $(b-a)/2^n$, sign invariant maintained, and $\varepsilon$-approximate roots found for any $\varepsilon > 0$. 13 theorems, 3 definitions, 0 axioms, 243 lines.
conclusion.implications: This formalization demonstrates that the classical IVT has rich computational content. Bisection is provably correct as a root-finding algorithm: it finds $\varepsilon$-approximate roots with $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ steps. The proof technique — extracting constructive content from classical existence results via compactness and uniform continuity — is a general pattern in constructive real analysis. In Bishop's constructive mathematics, the approximate IVT proven here holds constructively (no excluded middle needed), unlike the classical IVT which requires choosing a zero.
openQuestions: Formalize convergence of the bisection midpoints to an exact zero via completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ (Cauchy sequences), recovering the full classical IVT from the approximate version.
Prove the tight convergence rate: bisection achieves 1 bit of accuracy per step (linear convergence), and Newton's method achieves quadratic convergence — can both be formalized and compared?
Can the constructive IVT be proved in Lean without classical logic (i.e., in a constructive type theory), and what additional hypotheses on $f$ are needed?

crossReferences.description: The classical IVT whose constructive content this proof formalizes — proves the exact zero exists via Mathlib's intermediate_value_Icc
Companion formalization of the bisection method as a root-finding algorithm, focusing on the algorithm rather than the constructive content
Connection between IVT and Brouwer's fixed point theorem — another application of IVT-style arguments in analysis/topology

sections.title: Imports and Module Overview
sections.summary: Imports all of Mathlib. The docstring outlines four parts: bisection algorithm, width bounds, sign preservation, and the main approximate IVT theorem. Opens Set namespace.

sections.title: Part I: Bisection Algorithm Definitions
sections.summary: Three noncomputable definitions: bisectStep (one step: test midpoint, keep appropriate half), bisect (n-fold iteration by structural recursion), bisectMid (midpoint of n-th iterate). All noncomputable due to real-valued function evaluation.

sections.title: Part II: Width Bounds — (b-a)/2^n
sections.summary: bisectStep_ordered (ordering preserved, by split_ifs + linarith), bisectStep_width (width halves exactly, by ring), bisect_ordered (induction), bisect_width (induction: width after n steps = (b-a)/2^n). The key bisectStep_width needs no induction.

sections.title: Part III: Sign Preservation
sections.summary: bisectStep_sign: one bisection step preserves f(left) ≤ 0 ≤ f(right) by split_ifs + push_neg. bisect_sign: induction. Together they guarantee a zero exists in [l_n, r_n] at every stage.

sections.title: Part IV: Interval Containment in [a,b]
sections.summary: bisect_left_mono (left endpoint non-decreasing), bisect_right_mono (right endpoint non-increasing), bisect_contained ([l_n,r_n] ⊆ [a,b]), bisectMid_mem (midpoint ∈ [a,b]). All by induction + split_ifs + linarith.

sections.title: Part V: Approximate IVT — Main Theorem
sections.summary: approx_ivt: the main result. Uses isCompact_Icc for uniform continuity, exists_pow_lt_of_lt_one for Archimedean step selection, bisect_width + sign invariant for the ε-bound. The midpoint of the n-th iterate is within δ of both endpoints and bounded in f-value by both ±ε.

sections.title: Part VI: Monotone Exact IVT — Uniqueness
sections.summary: monotone_ivt_unique: for strictly monotone f with f(a) < 0 < f(b), the zero is unique (∃!). Existence via intermediate_value_Icc; uniqueness by contradiction from StrictMonoOn.

sections.title: Part VII: Constructive IVT Summary
sections.summary: constructive_ivt_summary packages three guarantees: approximate roots, midpoint containment, and width → 0. The third uses an Archimedean argument showing the bisection sequence is Cauchy, completing the constructive content of IVT.
